Let \(n\) have \(d\) digits, and write \(n=a_{d-1}\cdots a_0\). If any digit is \(0\), then \(p(n)=0\), so \(n=s(n)\), impossible for positive \(n\). Hence all digits are nonzero.

The condition gives
\[
\prod_{i=0}^{d-1} a_i=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1} a_i(10^i-1).
\]
The units digit contributes \(0\), so
\[
a_0\prod_{i=1}^{d-1} a_i
=9\sum_{i=1}^{d-1} a_i\frac{10^i-1}{9}.
\]
Since \(a_0\le 9\),
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{d-1} a_i\frac{10^i-1}{9}
\le \prod_{i=1}^{d-1} a_i.
\]
For \(d\ge 3\), using leading digit \(a=a_{d-1}\),
\[
a\frac{10^{d-1}-1}{9}\le a\cdot 9^{d-2},
\]
so
\[
10^{d-1}-1\le 9^{d-1},
\]
impossible for \(d\ge 3\). Thus \(d\le 2\).

For one digit, \(s(n)+p(n)=2n\ne n\). For two digits \(10a+b\):
\[
10a+b=a+b+ab \implies 9a=ab \implies b=9.
\]
So the coincidence numbers are
\[
19,29,39,\dots,99.
\]
Their sum is
\[
19+29+\cdots+99=9\cdot\frac{19+99}{2}=531.
\]
\[
\boxed{531}
\]
